extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political theory and European history
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting the criteria and evaluative principles the author uses to judge national development, national efficiency, and the relation between democracy and nationality in 18th–19th century Europe (with case studies of England, France, Germany).

rubrics_metrics.name: Nationhood measured by capacity for effective association
rubrics_metrics.description: “A nation is more or less of a nation according as its members are more or less capable of effective association.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text treats national strength as the ability of members to associate effectively (not racial or purely geographic ties). Long-enduring associations produce firm political structures, habits of joint consultation, and local traditions capitalized into national political life. Effective association requires mechanisms that make differences non-factious and enable collective action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of popular representation / government responsibility to public opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Political efficiency and responsibility both implied some degree of popular representation; 'the government should make itself expressly responsible to public opinion.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Representative institutions (even limited ones) are necessary for national cohesion; they do not have to be full democracy but must consult public opinion on important questions. The revolutionary period taught statesmen that some popular representation is indispensable to nation-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequate machinery of consultation and discussion
rubrics_metrics.description: National cohesion 'could be secured only by an adequate machinery of consultation and discussion' whose decisions determine political action taken in the name of the whole community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such machinery remedies grievances, mitigates factiousness, and adjusts individual and class differences. There is no universal form — machinery must be appropriate to local traditions — but its existence is essential to transform association into loyalty and fruitful cooperation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation and moderation of absolute authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Absolute authority created to preserve order can become a cause of 'internal and external disorder' if not properly limited; the Holy Alliance exercised power 'with moderation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authority must be keyed to public safety only where necessary; the abuse of 'La Raison d'État' for trivial domestic or dynastic ends is an anti-pattern. Effective government requires limits on arbitrary power and institutional responsibility rather than perpetual emergency rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alignment of political organization with legitimate national interests
rubrics_metrics.description: A national principle depends on 'the establishment and maintenance of a constructive relation between the official political organization and policy and the interests, the ideas, and the traditions of the people as a whole.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political institutions and policies must be adapted to domestic needs and national aspirations; failure to adapt (e.g., the Bourbons) generates a nation 'divided against itself' and weakens international standing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capacity to mobilize national energy and efficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: Revolutionary France 'released sources of national energy' and 'French national efficiency was temporarily so increased' when national cohesion and mobilization occurred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: National efficiency is demonstrated by the ability to unite the populace for great tasks (military, political reform). Both democratic and non-democratic systems can increase national efficiency if they harness popular energy, but excesses may provoke counter-reactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance between democratic infusion and national integrity
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'democratic infusion cannot at any one time be carried very far without impairing the national integrity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There must be a measured balance: some democratic reforms help cohesion and efficiency, but radical democratic destruction of national institutions can damage the bonds of association. The appropriate extent of democracy depends on historical context and existing traditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Particularity and historicity of national institutions (no universal machinery)
rubrics_metrics.description: A national policy and organization is 'essentially particular' because nations originated in local political groups with peculiar interests, institutions, and traditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutional solutions must fit local historical traditions and the international environment; grafting representative institutions onto tradition is the practical path rather than imposing a single universal model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Influence of international system and neighbors on national development
rubrics_metrics.description: Each nation 'was formed... as part of a political system which included other nations' and increasing national association forces neighbors into submission or into equal national resistance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A state's position and relations in the broader international system condition domestic capacity for nationalization; external pressures and competition shape what domestic reforms are possible or necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tolerance and institutional management of individual and class differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Loyal and fruitful association 'gains enormously from a wide variety of individual differences' provided such differences do not become factious; mitigation requires machinery of mutual consultation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Healthy nationhood tolerates diversity of conviction and interest, using institutions to adjust differences rather than suppress them; suppression was an older remedy but becomes untenable once order is secured.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic policy oriented to national interests (nationalized economy vs laissez-faire)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'system of national economy appears to make for a higher level of economic vitality than a system of international economy.' Britain’s resignation of economic responsibility harmed national vitality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Governments should not abandon economic leadership when national economic competition is fierce; overly individualistic laissez-faire (transferring economic responsibility entirely to individuals) can undermine national competitiveness relative to states that nationalize economic organization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Governmental leadership and responsibility for economic welfare
rubrics_metrics.description: The English governing class 'practically surrendered its primary function' by resigning economic responsibility at the very time national economic interests needed vigilant protection and promotion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political leadership entails active stewardship of national economic policy; abdication of this role (even if politically convenient) is criticized as betrayal of the national interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meritocratic standards and requirement for specialized competence
rubrics_metrics.description: The customary English standard demanded honesty, patriotism, gentlemanly conduct, courage, and being a 'good sort' but 'wholly failed to demand high special training, intense application, unremitting energy' necessary for modern efficiency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective national administration and leadership increasingly require specialized training, sustained application, and technical competence rather than merely social standing or general 'good' character; failure to raise standards is an anti-pattern that preserves privilege over merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of systemic social favoritism and hereditary 'pull'
rubrics_metrics.description: English social and political life is 'infected' with social favoritism; the system is 'constituted on the basis of a systematic and hereditary "pull."'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutionalized favoritism diminishes national efficiency by displacing more competent individuals; while some standards of character are necessary, overt nepotism and class-based entitlement are detrimental to national vigor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation in foreign policy and renunciation of aggressive expansion
rubrics_metrics.description: The Holy Alliance's system 'did not combine... to break the peace and prey upon a defenseless neighbor, but to keep the peace... it meant also the renunciation of aggressive foreign policies.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An international order that prioritizes preservation of the balance of power and restrains aggressive foreign policy can stabilize Europe and allow domestic national development; by contrast, states using expansionism for dynastic ends produce disorder.
